name: Jackfruit
subtitle: whole, fresh

base.tips: UH-CTAHR: fruit ripens in 3 to 7 days at 71–80 °F (22–27 °C). Keep it in a cool, well-ventilated place; fruit that fell from the tree lasts only 2 to 3 days.

CTAHR stores mature, undamaged whole fruit at 50 °F (10 °C) for 2 to 3 weeks. A 4 °C home fridge is colder than that, so expect nearer the short end and use cut flesh within 3 to 4 days in a sealed box.
Freeze the separated bulbs, not the whole fruit.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-19 – Jackfruit
UH–CTAHR F_N-36 – Quick Harvest and Postharvest Tips

notes: The 50 °F (10 °C) figure is a commercial storage temperature; a home fridge at 4 °C will chill the fruit harder, which dulls flavour. The freezer figure is a general practice for fruit pulp, not a CTAHR number.

name: Breadfruit
subtitle: mature green, whole

base.tips: Mature green fruit softens and turns yellow-green at room temperature in a few days. Let the cut stem drain its latex before washing.

CTAHR's optimum is 12 to 14 °C at 90–95 % RH for a maximum of about 20 days; chilling injury starts within 7 days even at 12 °C, so a 4 °C home fridge is well below the safe range and the fruit keeps only about a week before the skin scalds brown.
Freeze cooked and cooled flesh in portions rather than the raw whole fruit.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-37 – Breadfruit: Postharvest Quality-Maintenance Guidelines

notes: CTAHR's 20-day figure requires 12–14 °C, which a home fridge cannot hold. The honest home fridge range given here is shortened accordingly; the source figures are in tips. Freezer figure is general practice, not from the source.

name: Soursop
subtitle: whole

base.tips: CTAHR: the fruit softens 4 to 7 days after harvest and then has a shelf life of another 3 to 5 days. Handle gently — the skin bruises easily.
Only refrigerate once it has softened; chilling a hard fruit stops it ripening.
Freeze the sieved pulp; this is how soursop is normally kept for juice and ice cream.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-22 – Soursop

notes: The pantry and fridge figures come from CTAHR's softening-plus-shelf-life statement. The freezer figure is common practice for frozen fruit pulp, not a CTAHR number.

name: Atemoya
subtitle: whole

base.tips: Ripen unripe fruit at room temperature — CTAHR says unripe atemoya should be displayed at room temperature, never chilled.
Only once ripe. CTAHR allows ripe fruit at 2 to 5 °C, but calls the fruit very sensitive to chilling, which darkens the skin and strips the aroma; its commercial optimum is 10 to 13 °C at 90–95 % RH.
Freeze the deseeded pulp.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-38 – Atemoya: Postharvest Quality-Maintenance Guidelines

notes: CTAHR's optimum store temperature (10–13 °C) is a commercial cold room. Its explicit permission to hold ripe fruit at 2–5 °C is what makes the home fridge entry defensible. Durations are short by design because the source gives temperatures, not days; freezer figure is general practice.

name: Rollinia
subtitle: whole, biribá

base.tips: CTAHR: harvested fruit fully ripens in 5 to 8 days. Once the skin turns fully black the pulp goes clear and mucous and the fruit is edible for only 1 or 2 more days before it ferments.
CTAHR records a shelf life of less than one week; refrigeration buys a couple of days at the ripe stage but this Annona is chilling-sensitive.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-21 – Rollinia

notes: CTAHR states there are no formal postharvest studies for rollinia; its figures are Hawai'i field observations. No freezer method is listed because no source gives one.

name: Abiu
subtitle: whole

base.tips: CTAHR: full ripening occurs 1 to 5 days after harvest, once the pulp and skin lose their sticky latex.
CTAHR stores abiu at 50 °F (10 °C) for a shelf life of 7 to 14 days. A colder home fridge shortens this; the flesh browns quickly once sliced, so cut it just before eating.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-24 – Abiu
UH–CTAHR F_N-36 – Quick Harvest and Postharvest Tips

notes: The 7–14 day figure is for 10 °C storage, warmer than a home fridge.

name: Bilimbi
subtitle: fresh

base.tips: Very short-lived and easily crushed; do not stack more than two or three deep.
CTAHR: shelf life is up to 4 or 5 days, lengthening to 7 or 8 days when the fruit is chilled immediately at harvest.
CTAHR notes bilimbi can be dried or frozen for future use; dried fruit rehydrates in soup and keeps most of its sourness.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-23 – Bilimbi
UH–CTAHR F_N-36 – Quick Harvest and Postharvest Tips

notes: CTAHR says the fruit can be frozen but gives no duration; the 6–12 month figure is the usual home-freezer range for acid fruit.

name: Jaboticaba
subtitle: fresh

base.tips: CTAHR: no more than 3 days at ambient temperature before decay sets in.
Chill as soon as possible after picking — CTAHR says field pre-chilling adds more than a week of life. Waxing plus a plastic wrap extends storage to 21 days at 53 °F (12 °C) commercially.
Freeze whole; the skins slip off easily after thawing for juice or jelly.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-20 – Jaboticaba
UH–CTAHR F_N-36 – Quick Harvest and Postharvest Tips

notes: The 21-day figure needs waxing and a controlled 12 °C room, so it is quoted as a tip rather than used as the home range. Freezer figure is the general berry range, not a CTAHR number.

name: Langsat
subtitle: also sold as duku or longkong

base.tips: CTAHR displays langsat at 15 °C and says not to mist it. A cool, dry spot beats the fridge for this fruit.

CTAHR's recommended storage is 18 °C at 90 % RH for about 21 days, and it warns that the skin browns rapidly below 12 °C. A 4 °C home fridge is far below that, so the peel will brown within about a week even though the flesh stays good.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-42 – Longkong, Duku, and Langsat: Postharvest Quality-Maintenance Guidelines
UH–CTAHR F_N-36 – Quick Harvest and Postharvest Tips

notes: The 21-day figure is for an 18 °C commercial room, not a fridge. The home fridge range is shortened because the source explicitly documents chilling browning below 12 °C. No freezer entry: no source gives one.

name: Acerola
subtitle: fresh, Barbados cherry

base.tips: Extremely fragile; CTAHR packs it no more than two layers deep because a third layer crushes the bottom fruit.
CTAHR: postharvest life runs from about 4 days up to 10 days when the fruit is cooled rapidly straight after picking.
Freeze whole or as pulp; this is how acerola is normally kept for juice.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-36 – Quick Harvest and Postharvest Tips

notes: Freezer figure is the general soft-fruit range, not a CTAHR number.

name: Pitanga
subtitle: Surinam cherry, fresh

base.tips: Very soft skinned; CTAHR packs it no more than two layers deep in vented clamshells.
CTAHR: putting the clamshells into a cooler in the field can lengthen shelf life by as much as 10 days, depending on how ripe the fruit was when picked.
Freeze whole for juice and sorbet.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-36 – Quick Harvest and Postharvest Tips

notes: Freezer figure is the general soft-fruit range, not a CTAHR number.

name: Cape Gooseberry
subtitle: in the husk

base.tips: Leave the papery husk on. CTAHR notes that removing the husk reduces postharvest life, so de-husk only what you are about to eat.
Husked fruit should be packed no deeper than a pint container and chilled as soon as possible.
Freeze husked fruit on a tray, then bag.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-36 – Quick Harvest and Postharvest Tips

notes: CTAHR gives the husk rule but no keeping time for home storage, so the pantry and fridge durations are based on the FoodKeeper slug "apples" (a firm, low-respiration fruit with a protective skin), shortened for the smaller fruit. Freezer figure is the general soft-fruit range.

name: Salak
subtitle: snake fruit, in the skin

base.tips: Keep the scaly skin on and store dry and cool; overripe fruit turns tasteless and develops an off odour.
Loose in a paper bag rather than sealed plastic, which sweats and rots the fruit.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-36 – Quick Harvest and Postharvest Tips

notes: CTAHR describes salak harvest and grading and its overripe off-odour, but gives no home keeping time, so the durations are based on the FoodKeeper slug "pomegranate" — another hard-shelled, non-climacteric fruit that keeps well because its skin protects the flesh.

name: Sapodilla
subtitle: chiku, whole

base.tips: Ripen at room temperature until it yields to a thumb. CTAHR warns that fruit picked immature shrivels as it softens and never sweetens properly.
Refrigerate only after it has softened.
Freeze the deseeded pulp.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-36 – Quick Harvest and Postharvest Tips

notes: CTAHR gives maturity indices and the ripen-before-chilling rule but no home keeping time, so the durations are based on the FoodKeeper slug "sapote".

name: White Sapote
subtitle: whole

base.tips: CTAHR calls it highly perishable and soft-skinned; each fruit needs padding or it bruises.
CTAHR says to chill it in the field or as soon as possible after harvest.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-36 – Quick Harvest and Postharvest Tips

notes: CTAHR gives handling rules and the chill-immediately instruction but no keeping time, so the durations are based on the FoodKeeper slug "sapote".

name: Mountain Apple
subtitle: Malay apple, fresh

base.tips: CTAHR calls the mountain apple the most perishable of the Syzygium fruit and says it must be cooled in the field to get any postharvest life at all.
Single layer, padded, in a vented box — stacking bruises the thin skin.

sources.name: UH–CTAHR F_N-36 – Quick Harvest and Postharvest Tips

notes: CTAHR describes the fruit as highly perishable and requiring field chilling but gives no days, so the durations are based on the FoodKeeper slug "berries-blackberries-boysenberries-currant". Wax apple, the firmer cousin, is a separate record.

name: Black Sapote
subtitle: chocolate pudding fruit

base.tips: Ripen at room temperature until the skin goes olive-brown and the fruit is soft to the point of collapse — under-ripe it is astringent like a firm persimmon.
Only once fully soft; scoop the pulp and keep it covered.
Freeze the deseeded pulp.

notes: No agency or extension source with storage figures for black sapote could be fetched. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "sapote", adjusted for the fact that black sapote is eaten only when fully soft.

name: Mamey Sapote
subtitle: whole

base.tips: Ripen at room temperature until the flesh under a scratched patch of skin is salmon-pink and the fruit gives to pressure.
Refrigerate only after ripening; cut flesh browns, so press cling film onto the surface.
Freeze the pulp for batidos and ice cream.

notes: No fetchable agency or extension source gives storage figures for mamey sapote. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "sapote".

name: Star Apple
subtitle: caimito, whole

base.tips: Eat when the skin is dull and slightly wrinkled and the fruit is soft; the rind and the white latex near it are not eaten.
Whole fruit in a loose bag; it is non-climacteric so it will not improve after picking.

notes: CTAHR lists star apple but its text gives no home storage figures, and no other fetchable source did either. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "apples", a comparably firm-skinned non-climacteric fruit.

name: Santol
subtitle: whole

base.tips: The thick rind protects the fruit; keep it dry and out of the sun.
Loose in the crisper. Peeled segments should be eaten the same day.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives santol storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "citrus-fruit-lemon-lime-orange-grapefruit-tangerines-clementines", chosen because santol has a similarly thick protective rind.

name: Marang
subtitle: whole

base.tips: Marang ripens fast and is eaten within a day or two of the rind softening; the smell tells you when.
Separate the pulp segments from the rind and seal them in a box — the aroma spreads through a fridge otherwise.
Freeze the segments, not the whole fruit.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives marang storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "cherimoya", a comparably soft, fast-ripening tropical fruit.

name: Cempedak
subtitle: whole

base.tips: Strongly aromatic once ripe; keep it out of a closed room.
Separate the pulp segments and seal them in an airtight box so the smell does not transfer.
Freeze the segments; they are usually battered and fried straight from frozen.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives cempedak storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "cherimoya", shortened because cempedak is even more perishable than jackfruit, its close relative.

name: Pulasan
subtitle: in the shell

base.tips: The shell dries and browns quickly at room temperature even though the flesh inside is still good.
Seal in a bag to hold humidity — the loss of shell colour is water loss, not spoilage.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives pulasan storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "lychee", its closest relative in the dataset.

name: Mamoncillo
subtitle: Spanish lime, in the shell

base.tips: Sold in bunches on the stem; keeping the stems attached slows drying.
Bag them so the leathery shell does not dry out.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives mamoncillo storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "lychee", another thin-shelled Sapindaceae fruit.

name: Custard Apple
subtitle: bullock's heart, whole

base.tips: Ripen at room temperature until it gives to gentle pressure. Like other Annona fruit it is chilling-sensitive, so do not refrigerate it hard.
Only once soft.
Freeze the deseeded pulp.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives figures for Annona reticulata specifically. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "cherimoya", the same genus.

name: Indian Jujube
subtitle: fresh

base.tips: Keep out of the sun; the skin wrinkles and the flesh goes mealy once it dehydrates.
Bag them loosely in the crisper. Taiwan's winter crop is sold crisp and eaten like an apple, and that crunch is the first thing to go.

notes: No fetchable Taiwanese or other agency page gave a keeping time for fresh 棗子. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "apples", which matches how the fruit is eaten and how it loses quality.

name: Chinese Jujube
subtitle: dried, red dates

base.tips: NCHFP: most dried fruit keeps about 1 year at 60 °F (16 °C) and 6 months at 80 °F (27 °C). Airtight jar, dark cupboard, away from the stove.
Ohio State advises refrigerating dried fruit if possible; in a humid climate this also stops the dates going sticky and mouldy.
Double-bagged; freezing also kills any pantry moth eggs in a new packet.

sources.name: NCHFP – Packaging and Storing Dried Foods
Ohioline (Ohio State) HYG-5401 – Pantry Food Storage

notes: Both sources are for dried fruit as a class rather than for jujube specifically; Ohio State's shelf figure is 6 months at 70 °F, NCHFP's is 1 year at 60 °F, which is why the pantry range spans both.

name: Dried Longan
subtitle: shelled, longan flesh

base.tips: NCHFP: dried fruit keeps about 1 year at 60 °F (16 °C), 6 months at 80 °F (27 °C). Keep the sticky flesh in an airtight jar away from heat.
Ohio State advises refrigerating dried fruit if possible — worth doing in a subtropical summer, since dried longan is hygroscopic and moulds when it picks up moisture.
Sealed bag; thaw sealed so it does not sweat.

sources.name: NCHFP – Packaging and Storing Dried Foods
Ohioline (Ohio State) HYG-5401 – Pantry Food Storage

notes: Both sources cover dried fruit as a class, not longan specifically.

name: Dried Persimmon
subtitle: persimmon cakes

base.tips: Only for a firm, well-dried cake in a cool dry room. The white bloom on the surface is crystallised sugar, not mould.

NCHFP gives dried fruit about 1 year at 60 °F and 6 months at 80 °F, and Ohio State advises refrigerating dried fruit where possible. Soft, semi-dried persimmon cakes are moist enough that the fridge is the right default.
Wrap individually; they thaw in minutes.

sources.name: NCHFP – Packaging and Storing Dried Foods
Ohioline (Ohio State) HYG-5401 – Pantry Food Storage

notes: Sources cover dried fruit as a class. The pantry range is deliberately shorter than the source figure because commercial 柿餅 is semi-dried and much moister than the raisins and apricots those figures were written for.

name: Monk Fruit
subtitle: dried, whole

base.tips: NCHFP: dried fruit keeps about 1 year at 60 °F, 6 months at 80 °F. Keep the brittle shells whole in a tin; they crush easily and then absorb damp.
Airtight, to stop the shells softening in humid weather.

sources.name: NCHFP – Packaging and Storing Dried Foods

notes: NCHFP covers dried fruit as a class, not monk fruit specifically.

name: Buddha's Hand
subtitle: whole citron

base.tips: It is grown for its perfume, so a bowl on the counter is a legitimate way to keep it; the scent fades as the skin dries.
Loose in a bag. It is nearly all pith and zest with no juice, so it dries out rather than rots.
Freeze grated zest or candied strips.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives storage figures for Buddha's hand. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "citrus-fruit-lemon-lime-orange-grapefruit-tangerines-clementines".

name: Calamansi
subtitle: fresh, whole

base.tips: Thin-skinned and small, so they dry out faster than a lime on the counter.
In a sealed bag or box in the crisper to hold the juice in.
Freeze the squeezed juice in an ice cube tray; the whole fruit turns to mush.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives calamansi storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "limes", shortened at the pantry end because calamansi is smaller and thinner-skinned. This is distinct from kumquat, which is already in FoodKeeper.

name: June Plum
subtitle: ambarella, whole

base.tips: Eaten green and crunchy or ripened to golden and soft; leave it out to move from one to the other.
Green fruit keeps longer than ripe; bag it so the skin does not shrivel.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives June plum storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "plums".

name: Granadilla
subtitle: sweet granadilla, whole

base.tips: The hard orange shell protects the pulp; a lightly wrinkled shell means sweeter pulp, not spoilage.
In a bag so the shell does not dehydrate and crack.
Freeze the pulp with the seeds.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives granadilla storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "passionfruit", the same genus.

name: Curuba
subtitle: banana passionfruit
keywords: バナナパッションフルーツ

base.tips: Thinner-skinned than a round passionfruit, so it dries out faster on the counter.
Bagged in the crisper.
Freeze the pulp; it is normally blended into juice.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives curuba storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "passionfruit", shortened because the elongated fruit has a thinner rind.

name: Lulo
subtitle: naranjilla, whole

base.tips: Rub off the fine hairs before use. Like a tomato it ripens further on the counter and dislikes hard chilling.
Only once fully orange; cold storage of unripe fruit stops it colouring.
Freeze the sieved pulp — this is the normal form sold outside the Andes.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives lulo storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "tomatoes", the closest relative in the dataset and a good match for its chilling behaviour.

name: Tamarillo
subtitle: tree tomato, whole

base.tips: Ripens and sweetens off the tree; leave firm fruit out until it yields slightly.
Once ripe, bagged in the crisper. The skin is bitter and is always peeled or scooped around.
Blanch briefly, slip the skins, then freeze the flesh.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives tamarillo storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "tomatoes", the same family, extended slightly because the tamarillo's skin is much tougher.

name: Açaí Pulp
subtitle: frozen, unsweetened

afterOpening.tips: Thawed pulp oxidises fast and is meant to be blended straight away. Never refreeze it.

base.tips: Keep the sachets rock-hard at the back of the freezer, not in the door.

notes: Açaí is almost never sold fresh outside Amazonia; this record covers the frozen pulp packs. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "frozen-fruits". No fetchable agency source gives açaí-specific figures.

name: Cupuaçu
subtitle: whole or frozen pulp

base.tips: The thick brown rind protects the pulp; the fruit is normally opened as soon as it drops.
Scoop the pulp off the seeds and keep it covered.
Frozen pulp is the standard form outside Brazil.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives cupuaçu storage figures. The fresh numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "cherimoya"; the freezer figure follows FoodKeeper's frozen-fruit practice.

name: Chinese Bayberry
subtitle: fresh, yangmei

base.tips: Notoriously short-lived: the surface bristles collapse and the fruit weeps juice within a day at room temperature. Do not wash before storing.
Single layer in a vented punnet, not piled deep — the weight bruises the fruit underneath.
Freeze on a tray then bag; frozen bayberry is eaten half-thawed or steeped in liquor.

notes: No fetchable Taiwanese or Chinese agency page gave a keeping time for 楊梅. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "berries-blackberries-boysenberries-currant".

name: Sea Buckthorn
subtitle: fresh berries

base.tips: The berries burst easily; keep them in a shallow layer and do not wash until use.
Sea buckthorn is almost always frozen straight after harvest — the berries are usually shaken off frozen branches — and juiced from frozen.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives sea buckthorn storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "berries-blackberries-boysenberries-currant". No pantry entry: the berries do not keep at room temperature.

name: Quince
subtitle: whole, raw

base.tips: Quince is rock hard and keeps well in a cool room; a bowl of them will perfume a kitchen. Store away from other fruit, which picks up the scent.
Wrap loosely; the skin bruises brown where it knocks. Ohio State gives apples 1 to 3 weeks in the fridge, and quince, being denser and harder, holds considerably longer.
Freeze peeled, cored and poached — raw quince flesh browns and stays woody.

sources.name: Ohioline (Ohio State) HYG-5403 – Refrigerator Storage

notes: The Ohio State table covers apples, not quince, so the numbers here are based on the FoodKeeper slug "apples" and extended because quince is a much firmer, later-keeping pome fruit. Treat the fridge figure as an estimate.

name: Medlar
subtitle: for bletting

base.tips: Medlars are picked hard and deliberately left to blet — held in a single layer in a cool airy place until the flesh goes brown and soft, which is when they become edible.
Once bletted. Refrigerating them before they blet simply delays the process.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives medlar storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "apples" and reshaped around bletting, which is a ripening step rather than spoilage.

name: Ice Cream Bean
subtitle: guaba pods
keywords: アイスクリームビーン

base.tips: Keep the pod closed until you eat it — the white pulp around the seeds browns within hours of being opened.
Whole pods only, in a bag. The pulp itself does not store.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives Inga pod storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "beans-and-peas-green-fava-lima-soybean-wax-snow", the closest match for a fresh legume pod, though the edible part here is the sweet aril.

name: Camu Camu
subtitle: fresh or frozen pulp

base.tips: Extremely acidic and extremely soft; it is picked and pulped almost immediately in Amazonia and rarely reaches a market fresh.
Frozen pulp is the normal traded form.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives camu camu storage figures. The fresh numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "berries-blackberries-boysenberries-currant"; the freezer figure follows FoodKeeper's frozen-fruit practice. No pantry entry — the fruit does not hold at room temperature.

name: Canistel
subtitle: egg fruit, whole

base.tips: Ripen at room temperature until the skin is deep orange and the fruit gives all over; unripe canistel is chalky and astringent.
Only once soft. The flesh is dry and dense like a boiled yolk and dries out further in cold air, so wrap it.
Freeze the mashed flesh.

notes: No fetchable agency source gives canistel storage figures. The numbers are taken from the FoodKeeper slug "sapote", the same family (Sapotaceae).
